arguments.body:
PRIVILEGED & CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT
MEMORANDUM

TO: Engagement Team
FROM: Arbitration / International Dispute Resolution Practice
RE: Analysis of Counterparty Markup of Arbitration Agreement — Accept/Reject/Counter Recommendations
MATTER: Arbitration International Dispute Resolution — Counterparty Markup Analysis
DATE: [Current Date]

I. PURPOSE AND SCOPE

This memorandum analyzes the counterparty's redline markup of our arbitration agreement against (i) the original draft, (ii) the relevant SPA excerpts, and (iii) our internal playbook and firm precedent. The objective is to identify each deviation introduced by the counterparty, assess its legal and commercial impact, and recommend an accept, reject, or counter position for each. This memo is prepared as attorney work product in connection with the negotiation of the operative arbitration agreement.

II. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The counterparty's markup introduces a series of deviations from our original draft. While several changes are benign or market-standard and may be accepted, a number of material deviations would shift the balance of the dispute resolution framework in the counterparty's favor. Key areas of concern include: (1) the scope of the arbitration clause and carve-outs, (2) the seat and governing law, (3) the number and appointment mechanics of arbitrators, (4) consolidation and joinder provisions, (5) interim relief and emergency arbitrator procedures, (6) confidentiality obligations, (7) allocation of costs and fees, and (8) waiver of punitive and consequential damages. Each is addressed in turn below with a recommended position.

III. DEVIATION-BY-DEVIATION ANALYSIS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

A. Scope of Arbitration Clause and Carve-Outs
The counterparty's markup narrows the scope of disputes subject to arbitration by expanding the carve-out for equitable and injunctive relief and adding a new carve-out for disputes arising out of the SPA's indemnification provisions. This would fragment dispute resolution across forums and increase cost and delay.

Recommendation: REJECT the expanded carve-outs. Counter with language limiting carve-outs to urgent equitable relief necessary to preserve the status quo, and require that any carve-out dispute otherwise be resolved in arbitration. This aligns with our internal playbook, which favors a broad, single-forum arbitration clause.

B. Seat and Governing Law
The counterparty proposes changing the seat from [Original Seat] to [Counterparty Seat] and altering the governing law of the arbitration agreement. A change of seat can materially affect procedural law, court supervision, and enforceability.

Recommendation: REJECT the change of seat. Retain the original seat, which is a neutral, arbitration-friendly jurisdiction consistent with firm precedent. If the counterparty insists, counter with a neutral alternative seat and confirm that the governing law of the arbitration agreement remains the law of the seat.

C. Number and Appointment of Arbitrators
The markup changes the tribunal from a three-member panel to a sole arbitrator and alters the appointment mechanics to favor the counterparty's nomination rights.

Recommendation: REJECT the reduction to a sole arbitrator for a matter of this size and complexity. A three-member tribunal is consistent with the value and complexity of the underlying transaction and our internal playbook. Counter to retain a three-member tribunal with neutral appointment mechanics (each party appoints one, the two party-appointed arbitrators appoint the chair).

D. Consolidation and Joinder
The counterparty deletes the consolidation and joinder provisions, which would prevent related disputes from being resolved efficiently in a single proceeding.

Recommendation: REJECT the deletion. Consolidation and joinder are important to avoid inconsistent results and duplicative proceedings, particularly given the related SPA and ancillary agreements. Counter to reinstate the consolidation and joinder provisions.

E. Interim Relief and Emergency Arbitrator
The markup removes the emergency arbitrator mechanism and restricts the parties' ability to seek interim relief from courts.

Recommendation: REJECT the removal of the emergency arbitrator mechanism. Emergency arbitrator procedures are market-standard and provide a critical tool for preserving rights before the tribunal is constituted. Counter to retain the emergency arbitrator provision and preserve the parties' right to seek interim relief from courts where appropriate.

F. Confidentiality Obligations
The counterparty narrows the confidentiality obligations, permitting broader disclosure of the arbitration and its outcome.

Recommendation: REJECT the narrowing. Confidentiality is a core benefit of arbitration for this client. Counter to restore broad confidentiality obligations covering the existence, content, and outcome of the arbitration, with limited exceptions for legal process and regulatory requirements.

G. Allocation of Costs and Fees
The markup changes the default cost allocation from "the losing party bears the prevailing party's costs" to each party bearing its own costs.

Recommendation: REJECT the change. A prevailing-party cost-shifting provision is consistent with our internal playbook and provides a meaningful deterrent to frivolous claims. Counter to retain cost-shifting in favor of the prevailing party.

H. Waiver of Punitive and Consequential Damages
The counterparty expands the waiver of consequential and punitive damages to include categories that could undermine the client's ability to recover for direct losses.

Recommendation: REJECT the expansion. While a mutual waiver of consequential and punitive damages is market-standard, the expanded carve-outs would improperly limit recovery for direct damages. Counter to accept a mutual waiver limited to consequential and punitive damages, with an express carve-out preserving direct damages and fraud.

IV. OVERALL RECOMMENDATION

The counterparty's markup, taken as a whole, materially shifts the dispute resolution framework in its favor and should not be accepted in its current form. We recommend a comprehensive counter that (i) accepts the benign, market-standard changes, (ii) rejects the material deviations identified above, and (iii) proposes neutral, arbitration-friendly alternatives consistent with firm precedent and our internal playbook. Priority should be given to preserving the seat, the three-member tribunal, the broad arbitration scope, and the emergency arbitrator mechanism, as these are the provisions most consequential to the client's interests.

V. NEXT STEPS

1. Circulate this memo to the engagement team and client for approval of the recommended positions.
2. Prepare a redline counter incorporating the accepted and rejected positions above.
3. Schedule a negotiation call with counterparty counsel to resolve the material deviations.
4. Update the internal playbook with any market-standard changes accepted in this matter.

This memorandum is privileged and confidential, prepared in anticipation of litigation and negotiation, and should not be distributed outside the engagement team without counsel approval.
